title: A Local Geometric Analysis of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction via Error Bounds
claim: Gradient ascent on the objective converges linearly near a local maximizer, in both function value and iterate distance, across problem sizes.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, log-scale y, legend per panel
description: Two side-by-side line plots with a log-scale y-axis and iteration count (0 to 6000) on the x-axis. The left panel shows the function value gap F*−F^t. The right panel shows the iterate gap ||Z^t−Z*||_F. Each panel has three curves for d=64 (blue), d=128 (orange) and d=256 (green), listed in an upper-right legend. All curves start high and drop quickly. After a short plateau-like bend near iteration 700–1000, each curve falls as a straight line on the log axis, which shows linear convergence. The d=128 and d=256 curves fall faster and reach about 1e-12 near iteration 1500. The d=64 curve is slower and reaches that level near 3500. Faint grid lines appear. The eye goes first to the steep straight-line descents.
caption: Visualization of the convergence rate of gradient ascent for solving Problem (3). In both figures, the x-axis is the number of iterations, denoted by t. (Left) We plot the function value gap F ∗−F t against number of iterations, where F t = F(Zt) and F ∗= F(Z∗). (Right) We plot the iterate gap ∥Zt −Z∗∥F against number of iterations, where Z∗denotes the last iterate.
abstract: While the maximal coding rate reduction (MCR$^2$) objective has become a useful principle for learning compact and discriminative representations, a theoretical understanding of its optimization geometry remains limited, especially regarding why first-order methods often exhibit fast convergence near its local maximizers. In this work, we show that the MCR$^2$ objective satisfies an error-bound property in a neighborhood of its local maximizers. This property guarantees that the distance to the local maximizer set can be bounded above by the gradient norm at any point in the neighborhood, directly implying regularity conditions such as the Polyak--Åojasiewicz inequality and quadratic growth. Leveraging this property, we prove that first-order methods converge linearly to a local maximizer of the MCR$^2$ objective under mild conditions. Numerical experiments validate the predicted local convergence behavior and provide empirical evidence that optimizing the MCR$^2$ objective improves representation geometry while maintaining competitive downstream accuracy.
